system_description.narrative_title: Frayed Multipolar Order: AI, Energy and Hot-War Shocks
system_description.narrative_summary: The global geopolitical order is an open, tightly coupled system under simultaneous stress from regional wars (Middle East, Ukraine), high‑stakes domestic politics (notably US midterms), and rapid technological and market disruption (AI, chip shortages, crypto hacks). Those stresses propagate through energy and commodity markets, financial volatility and critical‑infrastructure vulnerabilities, producing fast feedbacks and nonlinear spillovers as states, firms and non‑state actors jockey for advantage. Great‑power competition and fragile diplomacy mediate escalation risks but also create new fault lines across trade, technology and security.
system_description.scope: Sovereign states, alliances and diplomatic channels; major corporations (tech, energy, finance); financial and commodity markets; supply chains and critical infrastructure (energy, shipping, cyber); conflict theatres and transnational non‑state actors; public opinion and media flows that influence policy.
system_description.super_system: The planetary socio‑political‑economic system (global human security and economic order integrating states, markets, technology and ecosystems).
adjacent_subsystems: Global financial and commodity markets (bonds, equities, oil, LNG)
High‑tech / AI-industrial complex (chips, cloud, AI firms, data infrastructure)
Regional security theatres (Middle East; Eastern Europe / Black Sea)
Energy production & global supply chains (oil, gas, LNG, shipping lanes)

variables.name: US–Iran military confrontation
variables.description: The United States, Israel and Iran are engaged in a cycle of strikes, threats and diplomacy that is shifting military posture and escalation risk across the Gulf and adjacent seas.

variables.name: Russia–Ukraine war and European security
variables.description: Russia and Ukraine, with NATO, EU and Western support, continue a high-intensity war marked by strikes on energy and infrastructure and negotiations that are recalibrating European deterrence and aid flows.

variables.name: US–China technology and supply‑chain rivalry
variables.description: The United States and China are contesting leadership in semiconductors, advanced computing, data and industrial policy through export controls, investment scrutiny and regulatory maneuvers reshaping global tech ecosystems.

variables.name: Global energy market instability
variables.description: Producers, traders and consuming blocs face volatile oil, gas and refining dynamics driven by uneven investment, production decisions and wartime disruptions that threaten supply reliability and price stability.

variables.name: US political realignment affecting foreign policy
variables.description: Domestic political shifts in the United States are changing alliance management, intelligence sharing, aid decisions and trade posture, producing broad ripple effects for partners and adversaries worldwide.
